name: Carrots
description: A popular cool-season root crop. For straight roots, they need loose, sandy soil free of stones.
tips: Keep the soil consistently moist to prevent roots from splitting. Cover the shoulders of roots with soil or mulch to prevent them from turning green.
succession: Sow a new batch every 2-3 weeks from early spring until mid-summer for a continuous harvest.
yield: One root per plant. A 10-foot row can yield 8-10 lbs of carrots.

soil.type: Loose, sandy, well-drained soil, free of stones.
soil.notes: Compacted or rocky soil will cause roots to be forked or stunted. Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which can cause hairy, forked roots.

temperature.notes: A cool-season crop. Germination is slow in cold soil. Light frost can improve sweetness.

storage.notes: Remove green tops before storing to prevent moisture loss. Can be stored in the crisper drawer or in boxes of damp sand in a root cellar.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Carefully thin seedlings to stand 2-3 inches apart. Crowding leads to small or misshapen roots.

careTasks.name: Apply mulch
careTasks.description: Apply a layer of mulch to keep the soil cool and moist, suppress weeds, and prevent green shoulders.

careTasks.name: Harvest roots
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting when roots reach a desirable size and color. Loosen the soil with a garden fork before pulling.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water deeply and consistently, providing about 1 inch of water per week to encourage straight root growth.

name: Radishes
description: An extremely fast-growing, cool-season crop perfect for filling in garden gaps between slower plants.
tips: Harvest as soon as they reach a usable size. Radishes left in the ground too long become woody and unpleasantly spicy.
succession: Key to a steady supply. Plant a small batch every 7-10 days during cool weather in spring and fall.
yield: One root per plant. Harvests quickly. A small patch provides plenty.

soil.type: Loose, well-drained soil with plenty of organic matter.
soil.notes: Consistent moisture is more important than high fertility. Rich soil can lead to lush tops and small roots.

temperature.notes: Very fast-growing cool-season crop. Becomes woody and spicy (hot) if left too long or grown in heat.

storage.notes: Remove greens and store roots in a plastic bag in the refrigerator. The peppery greens are also edible.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Thin seedlings to 1-2 inches apart to give roots room to swell.

careTasks.name: Harvest roots promptly
careTasks.description: Harvest radishes as soon as they are about 1 inch in diameter. Check a sample one before pulling the whole crop.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water frequently and consistently. A lack of water will cause roots to crack or become woody.

name: Potato
wateringNeeds: Consistent moisture, especially when tubers form
description: Grown from "seed potatoes" (small tubers), not actual seeds. The harvested crop is the underground tubers.
tips: Hill plants by mounding soil up the stems as they grow. This protects developing tubers from sunlight, which can turn them green and toxic.
succession: Not applicable. Plant main crop at once. You can plant an early variety for new potatoes and a main storage variety.
yield: 5-10 lbs of potatoes for every 1 lb of seed potato planted.

soil.notes: Prefers acidic soil, which helps prevent a common disease called potato scab. Avoid applying fresh manure.

temperature.notes: A cool-season crop. Tubers form best in cool soil. The foliage is very sensitive to frost.

storage.notes: After harvest, cure for 1-2 weeks in a dark, humid place. Then store in a cool, dark, well-ventilated location (45-50°F). Do not refrigerate.

careTasks.name: Hill soil around stems
careTasks.description: When plants are 8-10 inches tall, mound soil up around the stems, leaving the top few inches exposed. Repeat every 2-3 weeks until plants flower.

careTasks.name: Monitor for Colorado potato beetles
careTasks.description: Inspect plants for the distinctive orange and black beetles and their larvae. Hand-pick them into soapy water.

careTasks.name: Harvest 'new' potatoes
careTasks.description: Carefully dig around the base of the plant to harvest small, tender 'new' potatoes about 2-3 weeks after the plant has finished flowering.

careTasks.name: Harvest main crop
careTasks.description: For storage potatoes, wait until the foliage has completely died back. Dig carefully to avoid bruising the tubers.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water consistently, especially from the time plants start flowering until the foliage begins to die back, as this is when tubers are actively growing.

name: Garlic
description: Typically planted in the fall for a mid-summer harvest the following year. Each clove planted will grow into a full bulb.
tips: Plant individual cloves, pointed end up. Mulch heavily after planting to protect cloves through winter and suppress weeds in spring.
succession: Not applicable. Plant in fall for a single harvest the following summer.

soil.type: Well-drained, fertile soil with good organic matter.
soil.notes: Good drainage is critical to prevent bulbs from rotting over the winter.

temperature.notes: Requires a cold period (vernalization) of at least 4-6 weeks at temperatures below 40°F to properly form bulbs.

storage.notes: After harvesting, cure bulbs by hanging them or laying them on racks in a shady, dry, well-ventilated area for 2-4 weeks. Then trim roots and tops and store.

careTasks.name: Apply winter mulch
careTasks.description: After planting in the fall, cover the bed with a thick layer of straw or shredded leaves to insulate the cloves over winter.

careTasks.name: Remove flower scapes (Hardneck garlic)
careTasks.description: In late spring, cut the curly flower stalks (scapes) that emerge from hardneck varieties. This directs energy to the bulb. Scapes are a delicious bonus harvest.

careTasks.name: Stop watering before harvest
careTasks.description: Stop watering about 2 weeks before harvesting, when the lower leaves start to turn yellow. This allows the bulbs to start curing in the ground.

careTasks.name: Harvest bulbs
careTasks.description: Harvest when the lower 3-4 leaves have turned brown but the upper leaves are still green. Carefully loosen the soil and lift the bulbs.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water during active growth in the spring. Garlic has relatively shallow roots and appreciates consistent moisture. Stop watering when leaves begin to yellow.

name: Onions
description: A long-season cool-weather crop. Bulb formation is triggered by day length, so choosing the right variety for your region is critical.
tips: Long-day varieties for the North, short-day for the South. Stop watering when tops begin to fall over naturally. This signals the start of the curing process.
succession: Not typical for storage onions. Green onions (scallions) can be succession planted every few weeks.

soil.notes: Onions are heavy feeders. Benefit from a balanced fertilizer, but reduce nitrogen once bulbing begins to encourage bulb growth over leaf growth.

temperature.notes: Bulbing is triggered by day length, not just temperature. Cool weather is best for top growth, and warmer weather for bulb development.

storage.notes: Cure for 1-2 weeks in a dry, well-ventilated spot until necks are dry and skins are papery. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

careTasks.name: Begin hardening off seedlings
careTasks.description: Gradually expose seedlings to outdoor conditions over a week to prevent shock.

careTasks.name: Weed carefully
careTasks.description: Onions have shallow roots and do not compete well with weeds. Weed often but carefully to avoid disturbing the bulbs.

careTasks.name: Stop watering when tops fall over
careTasks.description: When the green tops begin to yellow and fall over, this is a sign to stop watering and let the bulbs prepare for harvest.

careTasks.name: Harvest when tops are brown
careTasks.description: Once the tops have completely withered and turned brown, gently pull or dig the bulbs on a sunny day.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water consistently to encourage large bulbs. Reduce water once the tops start to fall over.

name: Beets
description: A cool-season crop grown for both its sweet, earthy roots and its nutritious, edible greens.
tips: Each beet 'seed' is a cluster of several seeds, so thinning is essential. Harvest roots when they are between golf ball and tennis ball size for best tenderness.
succession: Sow every 2-3 weeks from spring through early fall for a continuous harvest of both roots and greens.
yield: One root per plant. A 10-foot row can yield 4-6 lbs.

soil.notes: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers which encourages leaf growth at the expense of roots. Consistent moisture is key for tender, non-woody roots.

temperature.notes: A cool-season crop. Can tolerate light frost, which can improve the flavor of the roots.

storage.notes: Cut off greens about an inch above the root to prevent moisture loss. Store greens and roots separately in plastic bags in the crisper.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Once seedlings are a few inches tall, thin them to 3-4 inches apart. The thinned greens are delicious.

careTasks.name: Harvest some greens
careTasks.description: You can harvest a few leaves from each plant while the root develops. Don't take more than 1-2 leaves per plant at a time.

careTasks.name: Harvest roots
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting roots when they are 1.5 inches in diameter. They are most tender when between 2-3 inches across.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water consistently. Fluctuations in moisture can lead to cracked or woody roots.

name: Turnips
description: A fast-growing, cool-season root crop grown for both its peppery roots and its nutritious greens.
tips: Harvest roots when they are about the size of a tennis ball or smaller for the best flavor and texture. Hot weather makes them woody.
succession: Plant in early spring for a summer harvest and again in late summer for a fall crop, which is often sweeter.
yield: One root per plant. Greens can also be harvested throughout the season.

soil.notes: Amend with compost before planting. Consistent water is essential to prevent woody, bitter roots.

temperature.notes: A cool-season crop. The flavor of the roots improves after a light frost. Becomes woody and bitter in heat.

storage.notes: Remove greens and store roots in a cool, moist place like a crisper drawer or root cellar.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Thin seedlings to 4-6 inches apart to allow room for root development.

careTasks.name: Harvest some greens
careTasks.description: You can take a few of the outer leaves for cooking, but leave plenty to nourish the growing root.

careTasks.name: Harvest roots
careTasks.description: Harvest roots when they are 2-3 inches in diameter. Don't let them get too large, as they can become tough.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water consistently. Provide about 1 inch of water per week to ensure they grow quickly and remain tender.

name: Rutabaga
description: A large, sweet, cool-season root crop that is a cross between a cabbage and a turnip. Flavor improves significantly after frost.
tips: Often called 'Swedes'. They can be left in the ground through winter in mild climates if heavily mulched for protection and easier harvesting.
succession: Not typical due to its longer growing season. Plant once in early summer for a fall/winter harvest.

soil.notes: Requires more nutrients than turnips. Amend soil with compost and ensure consistent moisture.

temperature.notes: A cool-season crop that requires a longer season than turnips. Flavor is much improved by several frosts.

storage.notes: Store in a cool, dark, moist place. Can be stored in the crisper drawer or a root cellar. Often coated in wax for commercial sale to extend shelf life.

careTasks.name: Thin seedlings
careTasks.description: Thin seedlings to stand 6-8 inches apart to allow the large roots room to develop.

careTasks.name: Mulch to retain moisture
careTasks.description: Apply a layer of mulch to keep the soil evenly moist and suppress weeds.

careTasks.name: Harvest after frost
careTasks.description: Begin harvesting after the plants have experienced at least one or two hard frosts, which sweetens the roots. Loosen soil with a fork to harvest.

careTasks.name: Watering
careTasks.description: Water consistently throughout the season. Provide about 1 inch of water per week.
